about: Trojans: bodies sharing a world's orbit at its L4 and L5 points, for any world round any star (package CO1). Which worlds can hold them, how wide the swarm is, how much a migration catches and how much stays.

references: Murray, C. D. and Dermott, S. F. 1999, Solar System Dynamics, Cambridge University Press: section 3.8, the stability of the Lagrangian points (L4 and L5 are linearly stable for mu < 0.0385, the Gascheau and Routh condition 27 mu (1 - mu) < 1). doi:10.1017/CBO9781139174817
Dermott, S. F. and Murray, C. D. 1981, The dynamics of tadpole and horseshoe orbits I. Theory, Icarus 48, 1: tadpoles within (8 mu / 3)^(1/2) of the shared orbit. doi:10.1016/0019-1035(81)90147-0
atoms.shown: μ = m / (M + m);  L4, L5 hold if 27 μ (1 − μ) < 1;  Δa/a = (8μ/3)^½

equation.name: Whether a world's leading and trailing points can hold Trojans, and how wide the swarm is
equation.formula:
mu = m / (M + m)
stable = if 27 * mu * (1 - mu) < 1 then 1 else 0
width = sqrt(8 * mu / 3)

mu.name: the world's share of the pair's mass

stable.name: 1 if the points 60 degrees ahead and behind hold things, 0 if not

width.name: how far a Trojan's orbit size swings, as a share of the world's

source.text: Gascheau 1843 and Routh 1875, in Murray and Dermott 1999: the points 60 degrees ahead and behind a world are stable while 27 mu (1 - mu) < 1, about mu < 0.0385 (one part in 26). Dermott and Murray 1981: tadpole orbits stay within (8 mu / 3)^(1/2) of the shared orbit
source.where: Murray and Dermott 1999 section 3.8; Dermott and Murray 1981 section 4

explain.curious: Any world drags two quiet spots round its star with it, 60 degrees ahead and 60 degrees behind. Small bodies caught there stay for billions of years, as long as the world is under about a 26th of its star's mass. Heavier worlds get a wider swarm.
explain.science: In the restricted three-body problem L4 and L5 are linearly stable for 27 mu (1 - mu) < 1 (Gascheau, Routh). Tadpole orbits librate about them with a maximum half-width in semi-major axis of (8 mu / 3)^(1/2) a (Dermott and Murray 1981). Jupiter: about 0.05; Neptune: about 0.012; Earth: about 0.003.

k.source: Lykawka, P. equation.name: Share of a stirred belt a world catches into its leading and trailing points

width.name: how wide the world's Trojan swarm is

steps.name: how many giant worlds sit between this world and the stirred belt

k.name: catch per unit swarm width, for the world nearest the belt

h.name: how much the flow of scattered bodies thins past each giant

share.name: share of the stirred belt caught as Trojans

source.text: Lykawka and Horner 2010: all four giants catch Trojans from the disc their migration scatters, Neptune most (1e-4 to 1e-3 of the disc), then Uranus (1e-5 to 1e-4), Saturn (below 1e-6 to 1e-5) and Jupiter (several times 1e-6 to 1e-5)

explain.curious: When a giant ploughs through a belt, every world nearby can catch some of the scattered bodies into its quiet points. The world nearest the belt sees the most of them; each giant further in sees fewer, because the ones before it have already flung most away.
explain.science: The catch is the swarm's width times the flow of scattered bodies reaching the world. The flow thins by a factor h past each giant between the world and the belt. k and h are fitted to Lykawka and Horner 2010's four ranges: Neptune 3.2e-4, Uranus 3.6e-5, Saturn 1.2e-5 (just above their range) and Jupiter 2.7e-6. Our simplification: fudge register CO-capture.

atoms.shown: share = min(1, c μ), or 0 if a neighbour disturbs

equation.name: Share of a world's caught Trojans that stay for billions of years
equation.formula: share = if disturbed > 1 / 2 then 0 else min(1, c * mu)

mu.name: the world's share of the pair's mass

disturbed.name: 1 if a neighbour shakes the swarm loose, 0 if not

c.name: share kept per unit mass ratio

share.name: share of the catch still there after billions of years

source.text: Lykawka and Horner 2010 (doi:10.1111/j.1365-2966.2010.16538.x): most caught Trojans are unstable and leak away. Schwamb et al. 2026 (doi:10.3847/2041-8213/aead9a): Neptune's long-lived swarm is 4 to 10 times Jupiter's. Nesvorny et al. 2013: Jupiter keeps about 7e-7 of the disc
source.where: Lykawka and Horner 2010 abstract; Nesvorny et al. 2013 abstract; Schwamb et al. 2026 section 1

explain.curious: Bodies are caught with a spread of swings. Only the ones whose swing fits inside the quiet zone stay; a heavier world has a roomier zone, so it keeps more. A world shaken by a heavier neighbour keeps none for long.
explain.science: The stable region is (8 mu / 3)^(1/2) wide in orbit size and about as wide in eccentricity, so its share of a catch spread over a fixed range grows as mu. c is fitted to Jupiter alone (2.7e-6 caught, 7e-7 kept: 0.26 at mu = 9.5e-4). Neptune then keeps 1.4% of 3.2e-4, about 6.5 times Jupiter's swarm, inside Schwamb et al.'s 4 to 10. Our simplification: fudge register CO-keep.

atoms.shown: disturbed if |P₂/P₁ · q/p − 1| < near and m_n ≥ heavy · m

equation.name: Whether a neighbour shakes a world's Trojans loose
equation.formula:
offset = abs(ratio * q / p - 1)
disturbed = if offset < near and mn >= heavy * mh then 1 else 0

ratio.name: the outer world's year over the inner world's

p.name: the nearest simple resonance, outer number

q.name: the nearest simple resonance, inner number

mh.name: mass of the world holding the Trojans

near.name: how close to a simple resonance counts as near

heavy.name: how heavy, against the world, a neighbour must be to disturb

offset.name: how far the year ratio is from the resonance, as a share

disturbed.name: 1 if this neighbour shakes the swarm loose, 0 if not

source.text: Mars keeps a primordial L5 group (de la Fuente Marcos et al. 2024, doi:10.1051/0004-6361/202449688). Only Jupiter and Neptune of the four giants hold long-lived swarms, though all four catch them (Lykawka and Horner 2010). Our rule: a swarm is shaken loose when an adjacent world at least as heavy sits within 3% of a resonance of order 3 or less
source.where: judged by this package against the Solar System; fudge register CO-neighbour

explain.curious: A heavier neighbour whose year nearly fits a simple ratio with this world's keeps tugging on the swarm at the same place, orbit after orbit, until the Trojans fall out.
explain.science: Saturn sits 0.6% from 5:2 with Jupiter, 3.3 times heavier; Uranus 2% from 2:1 with Neptune, 1.2 times heavier; Venus 1.6% from 8:5 with Earth; Mercury 2.2% from 5:2 with Venus. All four lose their swarms. Jupiter, Neptune, Earth and Mars have no heavier neighbour so near, and keep theirs. A judged rule, not a fit: fudge register CO-neighbour.
